questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] schema evolution and history replay on a queued ingest pipeline (pulse-net, docs/adr/0001-async-ingestion-durable-queue.md). Scenario: SDK v3 changes the event shape (properties move under a nested context object and the old flat fields are kept for one release), and it ships while live traffic runs at about 2,000 events a second. The same month a customer whose ingestion broke for a week asks you to re-ingest 30 days of their own exported history, about 26 million events, into the same project, some of which are already stored, and their monthly counts must not double. Write your design before you look: how the queued payload is versioned so old and new rows can both be read, what identifies an event across a replay, which fields a replay must preserve, how the backfill is kept from delaying live events, and what downstream consumers must be told. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Version the queued payload: a row is serialized at capture and deserialized later, possibly by a newer deploy, and a row the reader cannot understand is classed as permanently bad and dead-lettered without a retry. Put an explicit version in the payload and keep the worker able to read every version still in the queue.
keyPoints.quote: rows that can never succeed (unparseable payload, failed re-validation, vanished project) dead-letter immediately

keyPoints.text: [w3] A replay needs an identity per event: the export hands out each stored event's id, but the stored id is minted fresh on every ingest, so carry the source id through the replay and make (project, source id) unique; a replayed or twice-replayed event is then skipped instead of counted again.
[w3] Preserve the original timestamp: ingest stamps the processing time on any event that arrives without one, so a replay that drops the field moves 30 days of history into today's buckets.

[w3] Isolate the backfill from live traffic: one worker drains one queue in arrival order, so 26 million replayed rows enqueued ahead of live events delay every live event behind them; give the backfill its own lane (separate table or worker at a lower rate) and throttle it.
keyPoints.quote: The single-worker design serializes ingestion; throughput is bounded by one consumer.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Replay each person's history in its original order: replaying an identify that already happened changes nothing, but a property set overwrites, so an old set replayed after a newer live one would roll that person's properties back.

[w2] The definitions registry records first and last seen with the ingest time and keeps the first value kind seen for each property, so a backfill makes month-old names look new and a property whose type changed in the new shape keeps its old type; decide whether the replay should update the registry.

[w2] Downstream syncs assume new rows sort after their position; replayed events carry old timestamps and land behind positions already passed, so warehouse syncs over that month must be told to re-pull the window.

[w1] Check the export is complete before replaying it: the asynchronous export job stops at 50,000 rows, far short of 26 million, so the history has to be pulled page by page from the export endpoint and counted per day before and after the replay.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — replay day: the backfill starts at 09:00 on top of live traffic, the v3 deploy goes out at 11:00 while 400,000 old-shape rows are still queued, the replay tool crashes at 60% and is restarted from the beginning, the backfill sends with the customer's write key, and the customer's saved funnels for last month change overnight. What breaks first, and what in your design decides each failure?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A deploy whose reader understands only the new shape turns 400,000 queued old-shape rows into permanent dead letters within minutes; deploy the reader first (it accepts both shapes), switch producers after, and drop the old reader only when no old-version row is left.

[w3] Restarting from zero re-sends the first 60%: without a unique source id that is about 15 million extra events, with one it is wasted work only. Checkpoint the replay by the export page position so a restart resumes instead of starting over.

[w3] Live events starve behind the backfill: the worker takes the oldest rows first in fixed-size batches, so an identify sent live at 09:05 waits behind millions of replayed rows and every insight on today's data lags for hours.

[w2] Capture is rate-limited per write key in the X-Api-Key header (else per client address), so a backfill sending with the customer's key spends the same budget as their live SDKs and their real users start getting 429s; give the backfill its own credential or its own lane, and pace it.

[w2] Nothing is materialized: dynamic cohorts re-evaluate against stored events every time they are used, so a backfill changes last month's funnels, retention and cohort sizes retroactively; tell the customer before the numbers move.

[w2] A replayed identify that links two existing persons triggers a merge that repoints the loser's historical events, a large update in the middle of the backfill; expect it and keep the backfill's batches small enough that one merge does not hold the database for long.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your evolution and replay choices against the alternatives: an explicit payload version versus a tolerant reader, upgrading queued rows in place versus at read time, a separate backfill lane versus one queue with priorities, a unique source id versus deleting the window and re-ingesting it whole, replaying through the public capture endpoint versus an internal bulk path, and original timestamps versus arrival time. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The queued payload is the serialized event record, so that record's shape is the contract between two deploys. A tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields, default missing ones) absorbs additive changes for free; a rename or a change of meaning needs an explicit version and a converter, which is code you carry until the old rows are gone.

[w3] Deleting the window and re-ingesting it is simple and exact on paper, but it destroys live events captured in the window and the person merges they caused; a unique source id costs an index and a contract change, and makes any replay repeatable.

[w3] Replaying through public capture reuses authentication, shape checks and the one ingestion code path, at the price of the shared rate limit and queue; an internal bulk path is faster and isolated but must re-implement the validation and person resolution the public path gets for free.
keyPoints.quote: pushing rows through the same `CaptureService` the sync path used

keyPoints.text: [w2] One queue with priorities breaks the strict arrival order that identity depends on; a separate lane keeps live order intact but lets the two streams interleave for the same person, so per-person ordering has to be handled by replaying history before or around that person's live events.
keyPoints.quote: writes to the same person must apply in arrival order

keyPoints.text: [w2] Keeping original timestamps keeps every chart true to when things happened, at the cost of late data landing behind positions downstream syncs have passed; arrival time is simpler for syncs and wrong for every time-bucketed insight.

[w1] Upgrading queued rows in place is a long write against the hottest table during the very deploy that changes them; converting at read time keeps the queue untouched and retires the old converter once the queue holds no old rows.
